messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Photographer
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
  Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

Vignette:
Mika is a 53-year-old married man of Pacific Islander background who has worked for many years as a photographer, most often on location and around large groups of strangers. When he speaks about the period that changed him, he returns first to the feeling of being trapped with no control over who could come through the door. During an assignment, he was held captive for a period of time by men he experienced as unpredictable and dangerous. In the enclosed space where he was kept, he became acutely aware of bodies, doorways, and movement. He watched every shift in posture, every quick turn of a head or arm, bracing each time someone moved suddenly near him. He remembers how important placement became: where he sat, how close he was to a wall, whether he could see the entrance, whether there was any possible path out if the room erupted. He learned to scan people continuously, trying to work out who might become dangerous next, and he lived with his body wound tight, ready to react before he had time to think.

After he was released, those same habits did not stay in the past. Mika returned home to his wife and tried to resume work, but ordinary settings began to feel organized around the same questions that had mattered in captivity. Entering a restaurant, a studio, or a client meeting, he would immediately look for exits and plan how he would get out if something happened. He could not simply walk into a room and settle; he had to map it first. If someone else suggested a table in the middle of the room, he would feel exposed and uneasy until he could move to a seat that felt protected, usually somewhere with a wall behind him and a clear view of the door. He did not describe this as preference so much as necessity. To sit where he could not monitor who was coming and going felt to him like doing something reckless.

His work as a photographer brought these difficulties into focus. On shoots he was often required to move through crowded spaces, to direct subjects, and to work quickly while assistants, stylists, or clients crossed behind him or reached into his field of view. Sudden movements by other people put him immediately on guard. If an assistant stepped toward him too fast to adjust lighting, or a subject turned abruptly, Mika’s whole body jumped into readiness before he could tell himself where he was. He became known for insisting on arranging the room himself before beginning, positioning his equipment so he would not feel boxed in and locating the nearest exit before unpacking a camera bag. He spent a great deal of attention watching people, not in the observational way his profession once required, but in a narrowed, defensive way, alert for who might be unsafe. In crowded jobs he found himself tracking faces, gestures, and proximity more than the work in front of him.

At home and with his wife, the strain showed differently but just as persistently. His body felt constantly tense and primed, as if danger might break in at any moment. He would ask her, again and again, whether he seemed all right, whether she thought he was handling things, whether she believed he was safe. He also sought the same reassurance from people he trusted in other settings, asking versions of the same question until he could settle briefly. The relief never seemed to last long. He was not asking casually; he appeared to need someone else to tell him that what he was feeling did not mean immediate danger. His wife had begun to notice that before social gatherings or public outings, he would study the setting in advance and then question her repeatedly, wanting confirmation that the place was fine and that nothing seemed off.

Over the months, these patterns narrowed his life. He avoided some assignments that would require tightly packed venues or too many unfamiliar people moving unpredictably around him. Even when he accepted work, he arrived early so he could assess entrances, exits, and seating before others came in. Meals out with his wife became tense negotiations over where to sit. He knew these precautions could appear excessive, but from his perspective they were sensible responses to a world that no longer felt neutral. What frightened him most was the possibility of being caught unaware, of missing the one dangerous person in a room, of being trapped again because he had failed to prepare.

By the time he sought help, Mika was exhausted by the constant vigilance and by how much of each day was organized around safety. The immediate reason was a recent shoot in which several people moved quickly around him at once and he found himself so physically keyed up that he could barely continue. Afterwards he kept asking his wife if he was okay, and hearing himself do it seemed to underscore how far his life had shifted. He came to treatment wanting some relief from living in a body that never stood down, but also fearful of what it would mean to stop scanning, stop planning, or sit anywhere without first making sure he could get out.
